syllabus.quote: Explain set out purposes or reasons/make the relationships between things clear/say why and/or how and support with relevant evidence

one_line: Make a point, then add a reason for it with 'because', 'so' or 'which means', and repeat until you have covered the marks.

points.text: An explanation has two parts. First you make a statement. Then you give a reason, a purpose or more detail about that statement.

cites.quote: An explanation requires a statement or description followed by a reason or purpose or further expansion of that statement
Explanations require a statement and an expansion, which is often a reason but can be additional facts, to fully answer the question.
An explanation is statement of fact with a reason or expansion giving its purpose.

points.text: Some Explain mark schemes mark a point '(1st)' and the expansion under it '(1)'. The (1st) mark is for your statement. The (1) mark is only for the reason or detail you add to that statement. Of the question parts we counted, 38 of the 176 Explain parts from 2022 on (to March 2026) use (1st) in the mark scheme.

cites.quote: The sampling rate can affect the quality of audio files/how the audio sounds (1st) – because it captures sounds at discrete points (and not the whole sound) (1)
To define/specify the timing of the movement (1st)
Access control can be based on attribute of user within company (1st) – so that they can only access data appropriate for their job/task/role (1)

points.text: A point with no reason can still get its one mark, but no more. If every point you write is only a statement, the mark scheme can cap you below full marks.

cites.quote: A less detailed answer, such as 'they can learn at their own pace' can be given credit as it is a correct statement of the effect, but it lacks the detail to gain any further credit because it does not add an expansion
MAX two marks if answers are all only first marks.

points.text: Where the mark scheme links an expansion to a first point, the expansion mark depends on it. In one encryption question, the two further marks were only available to answers that first said the data is scrambled. In a 2-mark question, one full point and its reason can be the whole answer.

cites.quote: A relatively easy first mark was given for any answer that stated that the data is scrambled. Many candidates achieved this mark. Two further marks were then dependant on this answer.
Max two for one complete explanation

points.text: Join the statement to its reason with a linking word such as 'so', 'so that', 'because' or 'which means'. The mark schemes and examiner reports use these words to show where the reason starts. Write the link word, so the examiner can see where your reason is.

cites.quote: Can be adapted (automatically) in response to changing conditions/change of staff (1st) – so that new employees can have access (1)
The lower the sample rate, the smaller the file size (1st) – because there is less data stored (1)
A good answer would have stated that there is no central governing authority which means that there is no oversight or regulation

stating the task 'to check that the project has ended' should have been followed by a reason such as 'so that all stakeholders and clients can agree that no further additions or changes are necessary'

points.text: Do not just describe what something is. Explain asks 'why' or 'how'. Examiners say many answers gave descriptions and lost marks.

cites.quote: Most responses gave descriptive answers rather than explanations.
Responses that described what each server was did not answer the question.
there is usually little or no credit given for describing what the point or process is since this does not answer the question 'how'

points.text: Leaving out the reason is a common mistake. Short, vague phrases like 'store web sites' or 'makes the code more readable' do not get full marks.

cites.quote: A common mistake was to omit a reason or expansion to the response – the question asked for explanations
Vague responses such as 'store web sites' were not sufficient to be awarded marks.
a significant number only stated that comment make the code more readable so did not gain the full marks.

points.text: Use exact technical words. In one encryption question, about as many answers said encrypted data 'cannot be read' as said it 'cannot be understood'. Only 'cannot be understood' got the mark.

cites.quote: Many candidates made the point that encrypted data can not be understood, but an approximately equal number stated that encrypted data could not be read, and were not awarded marks.

points.text: If the question has a scenario, use it. Your reasons should fit the situation in the question, not just be general facts.

cites.quote: As with all scenario-based questions, candidates are advised to consider the significance of this scenario.
The full range of marks is only available to candidates for answers referring to the scenario in the questions.

points.text: Write explanations in full sentences, not bullet points of a few words. A sentence lets you put the point and its reason together.

cites.quote: Candidates should be encouraged to write full sentences and discouraged from writing bulleted, short statements in their responses. Descriptions or explanations can only be conveyed in full sentences.

question.quote: Mainframe computers were developed from the need for computers to process data in tasks such as carrying out a census. (c) Explain why mainframe computers are used to process the data from a census.

strong.sentence: A census collects a very large amount of data that has to be processed,

earns.quote: The amount of data that has to be processed is very large (1st)

strong.sentence: as countries tend to have a lot of people and each person adds more data.

earns.quote: as countries tend to have a lot of people (1)

strong.sentence: All of this data also needs to be processed in a short period of time, so a mainframe with a high processing speed is used.

earns.quote: All data needs to be processed in a short period of time (1st)

weak.answer: There is a lot of data in a census. Mainframes are very reliable.
weak.why: Both sentences are only first marks with no reason after them. The mark scheme says answers that are all first marks get a maximum of two, and the examiners said most answers stopped at 'a large amount of data'.

basis.quote: Typically, however, responses tended to focus on that fact that there is usually a large amount of data.

examples.note: Adding 'as countries tend to have a lot of people' turns a statement into an explanation and unlocks the third mark. Think about why the scenario (a census) needs a mainframe.

question.quote: Explain how each of these methods keeps data safe from unauthorised users. (a) encryption

strong.sentence: so that it cannot be understood by anyone who intercepts it,
which means the data is of no use to a hacker or any other third party.

earns.quote: of no use to a hacker/third party (1)

weak.answer: Encryption makes the data unreadable so hackers cannot read it.
weak.why: It does not say the data is scrambled, so the first mark is missing and the two expansion marks cannot follow. 'Cannot be read' is the wrong idea; the examiners wanted 'cannot be understood'.

basis.quote: Rather than making data unreadable, encryption puts data into a state whereby it can not be understood.

examples.note: One point and two linked reasons can earn all three marks here. The first statement is the gateway; each linked reason after it adds a mark.

thin_evidence: Explain is common (176 parts from 2022 to March 2026), so the evidence is broad. But only 38 of those mark schemes use the explicit (1st)/(1) labels; the rest simply list points worth one mark each. The cap for answers that are 'all only first marks' is written out in 9626_w23_ms_13 Q3(c). No other mark scheme found prints that cap, so treat it as a sign of how markers think, not a rule for every Explain question.
